guide.title: 1. What is a default?
guide.text: A loan is in default when its final status is Charged Off or Default. Fully Paid is the non-default outcome. Only resolved loans can be measured, which is why the validation window matters.
guide.label: See defaults in the explorer

guide.title: 2. How do we score borrowers?
guide.text: The scorecard gives points for income, debt burden, utilization, inquiries and other origination-time features. A logistic model turns those points into a probability of default. Higher scores mean lower risk.
guide.label: Open the applicant simulator

guide.title: 3. How do we turn probability into money?
guide.text: Expected loss combines probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default. A probability of default is not a loss rate: recoveries reduce the loss, and exposure determines how much money is at risk.
guide.label: Inspect expected loss

guide.title: 4. Why does the tail matter?
guide.text: Expected loss is an average. Capital has to survive bad years, so the Risk Lab simulates many correlated defaults and reads VaR and Expected Shortfall from the tail.
guide.label: Open the Risk Lab

guide.title: 5. Why does the window matter?
guide.text: A loan only has an outcome when it finishes. Recent vintages are incomplete, and measuring only resolved loans changes the sample. The primary window is the mature 2014-2015, 36-month test set.
guide.label: See the evidence

terms.definition: Money lent to a borrower that must be repaid with interest.
terms.why: Every row in this project is one loan, and the loan amount is the exposure used in expected loss.
terms.example: The explorer covers {n_oot} resolved loans in the primary mature test window.

terms.definition: A loan that ended in Charged Off or Default status rather than Fully Paid.
terms.why: Default is the event the PD model predicts and the event that creates credit loss.
terms.example: The primary test window has an observed default rate of {default_rate_oot}.

terms.definition: A loan with a final outcome: Fully Paid, Charged Off or Default.
terms.why: Loans still open at the snapshot date have unknown outcomes and are excluded from validation.
terms.example: The full snapshot has {n_rows} resolved loans; the mature test window has {n_oot}.

terms.definition: The A-to-G risk grade assigned by the original lender, not by this project's model.
terms.why: The lender's grade is a useful benchmark, but it is not available to an outside modeler at origination.
terms.example: The lender's own grade still adds about {auc_gap} AUC over the leakage-free champion.

terms.definition: Monthly debt payments divided by monthly income.
terms.why: It measures how much room a borrower has for another payment.
terms.example: DTI bins in the simulator run from low to high and each bin has a signed score contribution.

terms.definition: The share of available revolving credit that is currently used.
terms.why: High utilization can signal financial strain and is associated with higher observed risk here.
terms.example: The simulator shows utilization bins in percent and the test-window share of each bin.

terms.definition: Gross yearly income reported at application.
terms.why: Income affects affordability and is one of the scorecard inputs.
terms.example: The simulator labels income bins in dollars, from up to $26,000 to more than $90,000.

terms.definition: Whether the applicant rents, owns their home, or has a mortgage.
terms.why: Housing status is correlated with other risk factors and is used as a scorecard category.
terms.example: The simulator shows readable categories and their test-window shares.

terms.definition: The reason the borrower gave for the loan, such as debt consolidation or a credit card.
terms.why: Purpose is available at origination and can carry risk information.
terms.example: The explorer ranks purposes by observed default, predicted PD or expected loss.

terms.definition: The scheduled length of the loan, usually 36 or 60 months.
terms.why: Longer terms take longer to resolve, so the primary window uses 36-month loans only.
terms.example: The primary window is single-valued on term, so the Term tab is hidden.

terms.definition: The year or month in which the loans were originated.
terms.why: Different vintages face different economic conditions and have different resolution rates.
terms.example: The explorer shows Jan 2014 to Dec 2015 monthly vintages, alongside the 2014 and 2015 year totals.

terms.definition: The estimated chance that a loan will default.
terms.why: PD is the first ingredient of expected loss and the target of the scorecard.
terms.example: The calibrated champion's mean predicted PD on the mature test window is {mean_pd}.

terms.definition: The share of exposure lost when a loan defaults, after recoveries.
terms.why: Default does not mean losing the whole loan; LGD converts default into loss.
terms.example: The portfolio-level realized LGD is {realized_lgd}; loan-level LGD models did not generalize.

terms.definition: The amount outstanding when a loan defaults.
terms.why: A high default rate in a tiny exposure matters less than a small rate in a large exposure.
terms.example: The portfolio EAD in the primary window is {portfolio_ead}.

terms.definition: The average credit loss implied by PD, LGD and EAD. Expected loss uses the exposure-weighted PD times the portfolio-level LGD, reconciled to the headline expected-loss rate.
terms.why: It turns a probability into a money estimate that can be compared across segments.
terms.example: Expected loss is {el_rate} of EAD, or {el_amount}, in the primary test window.
terms.formula: EL = PD x LGD x EAD

terms.definition: The variation of losses around expected loss, usually measured as a standard deviation.
terms.why: Two portfolios with the same expected loss can have very different uncertainty.
terms.example: The simulated UL is shown next to EL in the Risk Lab.

terms.definition: The share of applicants accepted at a chosen cutoff.
terms.why: A cutoff trades approval volume against the risk of the approved pool.
terms.example: The cutoff explorer reports approval rate and bad rate together.

terms.definition: The default rate among a group, often among approved loans.
terms.why: It measures the risk that is actually accepted, not the risk of the full applicant pool.
terms.example: The cutoff explorer compares the approved bad rate with the overall default rate.

terms.definition: The score threshold at or above which an application is approved.
terms.why: Moving it changes both approval volume and the quality of the approved book.
terms.example: The published KS cutoff is marked on the cutoff chart.

terms.definition: The share of a distribution at or below a value.
terms.why: It places one applicant or segment in the context of the test-window population.
terms.example: The simulator phrases the result as 'Scores higher than X% of loans'.

terms.definition: A transparent points system built from a logistic regression on binned features.
terms.why: It makes the model auditable: each input contributes a signed number of points.
terms.example: The applicant simulator uses the published scorecard points table.

terms.definition: A score is a fixed base plus the points for each selected bin. Higher scores mean lower risk.
terms.why: The breakdown makes the arithmetic visible and reproducible.
terms.example: The simulator's 'Why this score?' table sums the base and every contribution.

terms.definition: The contribution of one scorecard bin to the total score.
terms.why: Points show direction and size; a positive value lowers implied risk in this scorecard.
terms.example: Each simulator input shows its signed contribution next to the control.

terms.term: Base score, base odds and PDO
terms.definition: Scaling constants that map log-odds to a points score: base score, base odds and points to double the odds.
terms.why: They make scores comparable and let a score be converted back into a probability.
terms.example: The current scaling constants are read from data.json.
terms.formula: factor = PDO / ln(2); offset = base_score - factor x ln(base_odds)

terms.definition: A bin-level transform that compares the share of goods and bads in a bin.
terms.why: It lets a logistic scorecard handle non-linear bins and monotone risk patterns.
terms.example: The published points table stores one WoE and one points value per bin.

terms.definition: A summary of how much a variable separates goods from bads across its bins.
terms.why: It is used as a screening rule before correlation and VIF checks.
terms.example: The pipeline keeps the scorecard parsimonious after IV, correlation and VIF filtering.

terms.definition: A model that maps inputs to the log-odds of a binary outcome.
terms.why: Its coefficients are interpretable and can be converted into scorecard points.
terms.example: The scorecard and the regularized logit challengers use this model family.

terms.definition: An ensemble of shallow decision trees fitted sequentially to reduce error.
terms.why: It is the champion here because it captures non-linearities that the scorecard misses.
terms.example: The champion LightGBM has an out-of-time AUC of {champion_auc}.

terms.definition: The champion is the selected model; challengers are alternative models compared on the same out-of-time window.
terms.why: It keeps model selection explicit instead of presenting one model as inevitable.
terms.example: The Evidence tab compares LightGBM, random forest, probit and regularized logits.

terms.definition: Input variables known at origination, such as income, DTI and utilization.
terms.why: Using post-origination information would leak the outcome and inflate validation metrics.
terms.example: The scorecard uses seven selected features; challengers use the wider leakage-free set.

terms.definition: Using information that would not be available at the moment a decision is made.
terms.why: Leakage produces impressive validation numbers that cannot be reproduced in production.
terms.example: The project excludes post-origination fields and treats lender grade as a separate benchmark.

terms.definition: How closely predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
terms.why: A model can rank well and still be badly calibrated; expected loss needs calibrated PDs.
terms.example: The project reports a null calibration result: isotonic did not improve the test Brier score.

terms.definition: The mean squared error of predicted probabilities against binary outcomes.
terms.why: Lower is better; it rewards both discrimination and calibration.
terms.example: Raw and calibrated Brier scores are reported side by side in the Evidence tab.

terms.definition: The average predicted probability minus the observed rate.
terms.why: It tells you whether a model systematically over- or under-predicts.
terms.example: The calibrated score under-predicts the observed test-window rate.

terms.definition: The probability that a randomly chosen default ranks above a randomly chosen non-default.
terms.why: It measures ranking, not calibration or business value.
terms.example: The champion out-of-time AUC is {champion_auc}.

terms.definition: A rescaling of AUC: Gini = 2 x AUC - 1.
terms.why: It is common in credit-risk reporting and easier to compare on a 0-1 scale.
terms.example: The champion Gini is shown in the simulator and the Evidence tab.

terms.definition: The maximum distance between the score distributions of goods and bads.
terms.why: It is used to pick a cutoff that separates the two groups.
terms.example: The published KS cutoff is marked in the cutoff explorer.

terms.definition: A measure of how much a score distribution shifted between two samples.
terms.why: A large shift warns that the model is being applied to a different population.
terms.example: The mature and censored windows report PSI in the Evidence tab.

terms.definition: A plot of true-positive rate against false-positive rate across every cutoff.
terms.why: AUC is the area under this curve; the curve shows the trade-off the single AUC hides.
terms.example: The Evidence tab reports the AUC and the confusion matrix at the selected cutoff.

terms.definition: A table of approved/rejected loans crossed with good/bad outcomes.
terms.why: It makes the cost of a cutoff explicit: rejected goods and approved bads are different mistakes.
terms.example: The cutoff explorer reports approved good and approved bad counts.

terms.definition: Testing a model on a later period that was not used for fitting or tuning.
terms.why: It is a stronger check than a random split because it respects the time order of lending.
terms.example: The champion is tested on the 2014-2015 vintages after training on 2010-2013.

terms.definition: The primary window is the mature 2014-2015, 36-month test set; the secondary window is the censored 2017-2018 set.
terms.why: The secondary window is shown only to quantify how censoring changes measurement, not to select the model.
terms.example: The explorer uses the primary window with {n_oot} resolved loans.

terms.definition: A loan whose outcome is unknown because it has not finished by the snapshot date.
terms.why: Excluding unfinished loans changes the sample and can inflate measured performance.
terms.example: The censored window has a much lower resolved share and a higher apparent AUC.

terms.definition: Hiding segments with fewer than {min_n} loans from rankings and coloring them as insufficient data.
terms.why: Tiny segments produce unstable rates and very wide confidence intervals.
terms.example: The map hatches small states and removes them from selection; hovering shows only the state name, while the Selection block holds the interval.

terms.definition: A range that reflects sampling uncertainty around an observed proportion.
terms.why: It prevents over-reading a difference between two segments with different sample sizes.
terms.example: Select a state or grade and read the Wilson interval for its default rate in the Selection block.
terms.formula: Wilson interval for a binomial proportion, 95% level

terms.definition: The data contains approved loans only, so rejected applicants have no observed outcome.
terms.why: A model fitted on approved loans may not generalize to the full applicant population.
terms.example: Reject inference is exploratory only and feeds no headline number.

terms.definition: Repeated random draws used to build a distribution of possible portfolio losses.
terms.why: A single expected-loss number cannot describe the tail; simulation can.
terms.example: The Risk Lab reads precomputed paths; the browser never re-simulates.

terms.definition: A model in which each borrower's asset return depends on one common systematic factor and an idiosyncratic shock.
terms.why: It creates correlated defaults, which is what makes portfolio tails thicker than independent loans.
terms.example: The simulated loss distribution is built from this single-factor structure.

terms.definition: The strength of the common factor across borrowers.
terms.why: Higher rho means defaults cluster, so the tail becomes more expensive.
terms.example: The rho slider moves across the precomputed simulation grid.

terms.definition: The shared economic shock that affects many borrowers at once.
terms.why: It is the reason portfolio risk is not just the sum of individual loan risks.
terms.example: The surface shows how the tail changes as the systematic factor becomes more important.

terms.definition: A what-if scenario that scales PD, LGD or both before simulation.
terms.why: It tests how capital responds to assumptions worse than the calibrated baseline.
terms.example: The PD and LGD sliders snap to precomputed stress points.

terms.definition: A loss quantile: the level that losses stay below in 99% or 99.9% of simulated years.
terms.why: It summarizes the tail with one number, though it says nothing about losses beyond it.
terms.example: VaR 99.9% is {var999} of EAD in the base-case scenario.

terms.definition: The average loss in the worst tail beyond a VaR level.
terms.why: It captures the severity of extreme losses that VaR stops short of.
terms.example: ES 99.9% is shown next to VaR 99.9% in the Risk Lab.

terms.definition: The full range of simulated portfolio losses and how often each level occurs.
terms.why: The shape shows skew and tail thickness that a single average hides.
terms.example: The histogram in the Risk Lab is the loss distribution for the current scenario.

terms.definition: Techniques that reduce simulation noise without changing the quantity being estimated.
terms.why: Tail estimates need many paths; variance reduction makes those estimates cheaper and more stable.
terms.example: The project reports stratified and antithetic variance reduction, including a negative result.

terms.definition: An asset-correlation value implied by the Basel retail formula for the observed portfolio PD.
terms.why: It is a reference point, not a replacement for the scenario grid.
terms.example: The base-case rho and the Basel-implied value are reported in the Evidence tab.
